title: Trump Agrees to Crypto Ethics Rules as Senate CLARITY Act Vote Looms
excerpt: The White House says the president accepted the 'most comprehensive' ethics provision in history, but key Democratic negotiators say they haven't seen the deal and question whether DOJ enforcement is enough.
body:
• President Trump has agreed to an ethics provision in the CLARITY Act that would limit how federal officials profit from crypto, clearing what had been the bill's biggest obstacle.
  • Key Democratic senators — Kirsten Gillibrand, Ruben Gallego, and Angela Alsobrooks — say they have not yet seen the text, and Alsobrooks called DOJ-only enforcement “unserious.”
  • The Senate has fewer than three weeks to pass the bill before the August recess; missing the window could push legislation into 2027.
  • Crypto markets rallied on the news — Coinbase stock jumped 11% and Polymarket odds for the bill's passage rose from 31% to 43%.

President Donald Trump has agreed to accept conflict-of-interest restrictions in the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act, removing what had been the single largest obstacle to a Senate floor vote on the most sweeping crypto legislation in U.S. history, according to multiple industry sources and a White House official.

The agreement, first reported by journalist Eleanor Terrett and Punchbowl News on Monday, came after a July 16 meeting between Trump, Republican Senators Cynthia Lummis and Bernie Moreno, and White House crypto adviser Patrick Witt. The provision would limit how presidents, vice presidents, members of Congress, and other federal officials can profit from digital assets while in office — a clause that had stalled the bill for weeks because of Trump's own extensive crypto holdings.

“The administration has agreed to the most comprehensive and wide-ranging ethics provision in history.”

— White House official, speaking on condition of anonymity

Democrats Left Out of the Room

Despite the White House's triumphant framing, the deal was struck without Democratic input. Senators Kirsten Gillibrand, Ruben Gallego, and Angela Alsobrooks — the three Democratic negotiators whose votes are essential to clear the 60-vote cloture threshold — told reporters they had not been briefed on the provision's specifics, according to CoinDesk.

Alsobrooks was blunt in her assessment. She told Crypto In America that an ethics enforcement mechanism relying solely on the Department of Justice is “unserious,” pointing to the unusual position created by Trump's appointment of loyalists across federal law enforcement. Todd Blanche, the president's personal lawyer, is currently facing a confirmation process to lead the DOJ.

“We cannot allow members of Congress, senior administration officials, presidents or vice presidents to get rich off of these industries because of their insider status. It is the worst form of pay-for-play.”

— Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), at Consensus Miami 2026

Compass Point Research analyst Ed Groshans echoed the concern in a Tuesday research note: “The lack of state AG enforcement authority may prove to be a hurdle to achieving bipartisan support for the Clarity Act.”

What the Bill Does — and Why Ethics Became the Bottleneck

The CLARITY Act would give the Commodity Futures Trading Commission primary authority over digital commodity spot markets while leaving the Securities and Exchange Commission in charge of investment-contract assets, drawing a jurisdictional line that has never existed in U.S. statute. The House passed its version in July 2025 by a vote of 294-134, and the Senate Banking Committee advanced its text in May by 15-9.

The ethics question became politically charged because Trump's own financial disclosures showed he made more than $1 billion in 2025 from crypto-related ventures, including his family's company World Liberty Financial and a personal memecoin. Gillibrand, who has led bipartisan crypto legislation efforts for years, recently proposed banning all elected officials and their spouses from issuing digital assets, a measure aimed squarely at the president.

Senators Gallego and Alsobrooks, the only Democrats to help move the bill out of committee, conditioned their floor support on strong conflict-of-interest rules. Without them, the math doesn't work.

Markets React, Deadlines Tighten

Crypto markets responded swiftly. Bitcoin traded near $66,300 on Tuesday, up about 3% in 24 hours. Coinbase stock surged 11% to $178.64, while stablecoin issuer Circle jumped 7.6% to $70.44, according to Barron's. On Polymarket, the odds of the CLARITY Act passing in 2026 rose from 31% to 43%.

The legislative calendar is unforgiving. The Senate departs for its August recess after the first week of the month, and once lawmakers scatter, the focus shifts to November's midterm elections. If Democrats win control of either chamber, the bill could be shelved until 2027. Full legislative text is expected as soon as Wednesday, though that timeline has slipped repeatedly.

Patrick Witt, the White House Crypto Council's executive director, deferred his scheduled Army National Guard training to remain in Washington for the push — a signal the administration views passage as achievable.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For the roughly 4.4 million Indian Americans in the United States, many of whom work in the financial technology and crypto sectors, the bill's outcome carries practical weight. A settled regulatory framework could boost hiring at exchanges and DeFi platforms, and it would provide clarity for NRI investors holding crypto assets across U.S. and Indian jurisdictions.

What's Next

The full bill text, including the ethics provision, is expected to circulate among senators this week. Senate Majority Leader John Thune has said he intends to push for a floor vote before the recess regardless. The coming days will determine whether Democrats accept the compromise or hold the line for tougher enforcement — and whether the most significant crypto law in American history passes this Congress or waits for the next one.
